The curie is a unit of **activity** - the number of nuclear disintegrations per second.
**The definition.**
**1 curie (Ci) = 3·7 x 10¹⁰ disintegrations per second** ✓
**Where the number comes from.** It was originally fixed as the activity of **one gram
of radium-226** ✓ Radium has a half-life of 1600 years, and a gram of it decays at very
close to 3·7 x 10¹⁰ nuclei per second. The unit honours Marie and Pierre Curie, who
isolated the element.
**The SI unit, for comparison.** The **becquerel (Bq)** is one disintegration per second,
so
1 Ci = **3·7 x 10¹⁰ Bq** ✓
The curie is an enormous unit by that measure, which is why medical and laboratory
sources are quoted in millicuries (mCi) and microcuries (µCi).
**A sense of the scale.** A smoke detector's americium source is about **1 µCi**; a
hospital's therapy source may be several thousand curies ✓ One full curie is a seriously
hazardous amount of material.
**What activity does and does not tell you.** It counts **decays per second**, not the
energy released or the biological harm done ✓ Those need the gray and the sievert; a
curie of alpha emitter and a curie of gamma emitter are very different hazards.
**Reading the distractors.** **3·7 x 10⁷** ✗ and **3·7 x 10¹³** ✗ carry the right
mantissa with the wrong power of ten - the figure to fix in memory is the exponent
**10**. **None of these** ✗ is unnecessary once the correct value is recognised ✓
**A related unit worth knowing.** The **rutherford**, now obsolete, was 10⁶
disintegrations per second ✓ so 1 Ci = 3·7 x 10⁴ rutherford.
∴ 3·7 x 10¹⁰.

The caesium atomic clock is the standard that **defines the second**, and its precision
is about one part in 10¹³.
**The figure.** A caesium clock keeps time to roughly **1 part in 10¹³** ✓ which amounts
to an error of about **one second in 300,000 years** - or, put another way, about
3 microseconds per year.
**How the clock works.** It is tuned to a particular transition between two hyperfine
levels of the ground state of the **caesium-133** atom ✓ Since 1967 the second has been
**defined** as the duration of **9,192,631,770 periods** of the radiation emitted in
that transition.
**Why an atomic transition is used as the standard.** Every caesium-133 atom in the
universe is identical, and its energy levels cannot drift, wear out or be affected by
temperature in the way a pendulum or a quartz crystal can ✓ The standard is therefore
reproducible in any laboratory, without comparison to a master copy.
**What it replaced.** The second was previously defined astronomically, as a fraction of
the mean solar day ✓ But the Earth's rotation is **irregular** - slowing by about
1·7 milliseconds per century, with seasonal wobbles - so it is a poorer clock than an
atom. Leap seconds are now inserted to keep atomic time in step with the Earth.
**What it makes possible.** GPS needs timing good to nanoseconds, since light travels
30 cm in a nanosecond ✓ Satellite navigation, telecommunications and radio astronomy all
rest on clocks of this accuracy.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 part in 10⁷** ✗ is the accuracy of a good quartz watch,
a million times poorer. **1 part in 10⁻⁷** ✗ and **1 part in 10⁻¹³** ✗ are written
upside down - an "accuracy of 1 part in 10⁻⁷" would mean an error ten million times the
measured value ✓
∴ 1 part in 10¹³.

Read the dimensional formula term by term: **mass to the first power, volume to the
minus one**.
**Step 1 — interpret [M¹ L⁻³ T⁰].**
**M¹** - one factor of mass
**L⁻³** - divided by a volume
**T⁰** - no time dependence at all ✓
So the quantity is **mass per unit volume**.
**Step 2 — name it.** Mass per unit volume is **density** ✓
**Step 3 — confirm with the unit.** Density is measured in **kg m⁻³**, whose dimensions
are exactly M L⁻³ ✓
**Testing the other options.**
**specific gravity** ✗ is the **ratio** of a density to the density of water, so it is a
pure number - dimensions [M⁰L⁰T⁰]. Every dimension vanishes, which does not match.
**linear mass density** ✗ is mass per unit **length**, kg m⁻¹, with dimensions
[M L⁻¹ T⁰] ✓ The power of L is −1, not −3.
**impulse** ✗ is force x time, with dimensions [M L T⁻¹] - and it has a non-zero power of
T, which [M L⁻³ T⁰] does not ✓ That single observation eliminates it at once.
**The quick way to use T⁰.** A zero power of time means the quantity involves no rate,
no velocity and no force ✓ That removes impulse immediately, leaving only the three
mass-per-something candidates to distinguish by the power of L.
**Typical values, for a sense of scale.**
water: **1000 kg m⁻³**
air: **1·29 kg m⁻³**
mercury: **13600 kg m⁻³** ✓
**A caution on "specific gravity".** Despite the name, it is dimensionless - the word
"specific" in physics usually signals that something has been divided out ✓
∴ density.

Conductance is the **reciprocal of resistance**, so find the dimensions of resistance
first and invert them.
**Step 1 — get resistance from Ohm's law.**
R = V/I
and V = W/q, the work done per unit charge:
[V] = [ML²T⁻²]/[AT] = **[M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹]**
so
[R] = [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹]/[A] = **[M L² T⁻³ A⁻²]**
**Step 2 — invert for conductance.** G = 1/R, so every exponent changes sign:
**[G] = [M⁻¹ L⁻² T³ A²]** ✓
**Step 3 — check against the unit.** Conductance is measured in **siemens**,
S = Ω⁻¹ = A/V ✓ and
[A]/[M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹] = [M⁻¹ L⁻² T³ A²] ✓ the same result by a second route.
**A third check, through power.** P = I²R, so
[R] = [M L² T⁻³]/[A²] = **[M L² T⁻³ A⁻²]** ✓ consistent again.
**How to spot the answer quickly.** Conductance must have the **exact reciprocal**
dimensions of resistance, so the signs of all four exponents flip ✓ Finding the option
whose M and L powers are **negative** and whose T and A powers are **positive** narrows
the field to one.
**Reading the distractors.**
**[M¹ L² T⁻³ A²]** ✗ has the mass and length powers of **resistance**, not its
reciprocal, and the sign of A is wrong too.
**[M⁻¹ L⁻² T⁻³ A²]** ✗ differs only in the sign of the time exponent - the single
commonest slip, since T³ against T⁻³ is easy to misread ✓
**[M⁻¹ L⁻² T³ A⁻²]** ✗ has the current exponent negative; inverting resistance must make
it **positive**.
**The related quantities.** **Conductivity** σ = 1/ρ has dimensions [M⁻¹L⁻³T³A²], one
further power of length down, and **capacitance** has [M⁻¹L⁻²T⁴A²] ✓ Keeping the powers
of T straight is what separates them.
∴ [M⁻¹ L⁻² T³ A²].

Averaging reduces random error, and the reduction here is taken to go as **1/n**.
**Step 1 — state the rule used.** The random error in an arithmetic mean falls as the
number of observations rises:
error ∝ **1/n**
**Step 2 — compare the two cases.** Going from 100 observations to 500 multiplies n by
**5**, so the error is divided by 5:
new error = **x/5** ✓
**Why averaging helps at all.** Random errors are as likely to be positive as negative ✓
In a sum they partly cancel, and the more readings there are, the more complete the
cancellation. **Systematic** errors do not behave this way - a mis-zeroed instrument
biases every reading in the same direction, and no amount of averaging removes it.
**A worked instance.** If 100 readings give a mean with a random error of 0·2 units, then
500 readings of the same quality give
0·2/5 = **0·04 units** ✓ a fivefold improvement for five times the work.
**The practical lesson.** Reducing random error costs effort in direct proportion ✓ To
halve the error you must take twice as many readings; to reduce it tenfold, ten times as
many. There is a point beyond which it is better to improve the **instrument** than to
keep repeating the measurement, because the systematic error then dominates and further
readings buy nothing.
**Reading the distractors.** **5x** ✗ and **25x** ✗ have the error **growing** with more
observations, which is the opposite of why anyone repeats a measurement ✓ **x/25** ✗
divides by 5² rather than 5.
**A note on the rule.** Statistical theory gives the standard error of the mean as
σ/√n, which would reduce the error by √5 ≈ 2·24 ✓ The textbook treatment used here takes
the simpler 1/n dependence, and the options are built on it - only x/5 appears, with no
x/√5 among them.
∴ x/5.

Compute the area, then round it to the number of significant figures the **measurement**
justifies.
**Step 1 — count the significant figures in the data.** The side is 3·784 m - **four
significant figures** ✓
**Step 2 — compute the surface area.** A cube has six square faces:
A = 6a²
= 6(3·784)²
= 6(14·318656)
= **85·911936 m²**
**Step 3 — round to four significant figures.** A product can carry no more significant
figures than the least precise factor, which has four:
**A = 85·91 m²** ✓
**Why the extra digits must be discarded.** The side is known only to the nearest
millimetre, so writing 85·911936 m² claims a precision of a **millionth** of a square
metre ✓ That precision does not exist in the data; carrying it is a false claim, not a
more accurate answer.
**How much the uncertainty really is.** If a = 3·784 ± 0·001 m, the fractional error in a
is 0·026%, and the area carries **twice** that, 0·053% ✓ On 85·91 m² that is about
**±0·05 m²** - so even the second decimal place is marginal, and the fourth significant
figure is the honest limit.
**The rule for multiplication.** The result keeps the **smallest number of significant
figures** among the factors ✓ The exact 6 is a counted number, not a measurement, so it
imposes no limit.
**Contrast with addition.** For sums the rule is about **decimal places**, not
significant figures ✓ Mixing the two rules is the usual source of error in this topic.
**Reading the distractors.** **85·911936 m²** ✗ is the raw calculator output, with eight
figures. **85·9119 m²** ✗ keeps six, and **85·911 m²** ✗ keeps five - all three claim
more precision than the measurement supports ✓
∴ 85·91 m², which is the fourth option (printed there as 89·91 m², a slip in the second
digit - the computed value is 6 x 3·784² = 85·911936, rounding to 85·91).

When two quantities are **subtracted**, their absolute errors **add**.
**Step 1 — state the quantities.** Let
A = a ± Δa and B = b ± Δb
and form the difference X = A − B.
**Step 2 — find the extreme values.** The difference is largest when A is at its
greatest and B at its least, and smallest in the reverse case:
X_max = (a + Δa) − (b − Δb) = (a − b) + **(Δa + Δb)**
X_min = (a − Δa) − (b + Δb) = (a − b) − **(Δa + Δb)**
**Step 3 — read off the error.**
**ΔX = Δa + Δb** - the **sum** of the absolute errors ✓
**Why errors add rather than cancel.** The errors are unknown in **sign** ✓ We cannot
assume one will offset the other, so we must allow for the worst case, in which they
reinforce. Subtracting the errors would assume a cancellation we have no right to expect.
**Why the rule is the same for sums and differences.** For X = A + B the same working
gives ΔX = Δa + Δb ✓ Whether the quantities are added or subtracted, their **absolute**
errors always add.
**A numerical instance.** Take A = 10·0 ± 0·2 and B = 9·0 ± 0·3:
difference = **1·0**, with error 0·2 + 0·3 = **±0·5** ✓
so the result is 1·0 ± 0·5 - a **50%** uncertainty, though each original measurement was
good to a few per cent.
**The practical warning.** Subtracting two nearly equal quantities is dangerous ✓ The
difference shrinks while the error does not, so the **relative** error can become
enormous. Good experimental design avoids measuring a small quantity as the difference of
two large ones.
**Reading the distractors.** **Difference of the absolute errors** ✗ assumes a
cancellation that cannot be relied on, and would give zero error for equally uncertain
quantities. **Product of the errors** ✗ is dimensionally wrong - the product of two
lengths is not a length ✓ **None of the above** ✗ is unnecessary.
**The companion rules.** For **products and quotients**, it is the **relative** errors
that add; for a **power** xⁿ, the relative error is multiplied by n ✓
∴ sum of absolute errors in the two quantities.
